edges.description: Germinating spores become vegetative bacilli that escape macrophage phagocytic vesicles.
Escaped vegetative bacilli activate capsule synthesis and resist phagocytic clearance.
Extracellular bacilli secrete protective antigen with lethal factor and edema factor.
Once PA delivers lethal factor into the cytosol, lethal factor perturbs host MAPK signaling.
PA also delivers edema factor into host cells, where edema toxin activity begins.
Lethal-toxin activity in the vasculature drives endothelial cell apoptosis.
Toxin-driven immune suppression permits unchecked bacterial proliferation and systemic toxemia.
Edema toxin activity and vascular injury produce prominent tissue edema.
Endothelial injury and capillary leak drive hypotension and shock in systemic anthrax.
Local toxin activity and tissue injury at a skin inoculation site produce the eschar of cutaneous anthrax.
Systemic toxemia produces fever across the portal-of-entry forms.
Regional and systemic spread produces lymphadenopathy, associated with early fatal outcomes.
Mediastinal disease and pleural effusions in inhalational anthrax cause dyspnea.
Inhalational anthrax characteristically produces large, lethal-factor-rich pleural effusions.
Reaccumulating pleural effusions and systemic toxemia can progress to respiratory failure.
Ingestion anthrax commonly produces massive ascites, a further lethal-factor reservoir.
Systemic vegetative growth and toxemia manifest as sepsis.
Disseminated bacilli can invade the meninges and produce anthrax meningitis.
Intestinal mucosal infection and edema produce abdominal pain in gastrointestinal anthrax.
Gastrointestinal anthrax produces nausea and vomiting during intestinal disease.

nodes.description: Intestinal anthrax can progress to acute abdominal pain as lesions develop along the gastrointestinal tract.

evidence.reference_title: Human Anthrax: Update of the Diagnosis and Treatment.
evidence.snippet: As the infection progresses, symptoms include acute abdominal pain, hematemesis, bloody diarrhea and massive ascites followed by toxemia and shock which results in death.

nodes.description: Antitoxins such as anthrax immunoglobulin intravenous, obiltoxaximab, and raxibacumab neutralize circulating toxin and are considered adjunctive countermeasures for systemic anthrax.

evidence.reference_title: CDC Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Anthrax, 2023.
evidence.snippet: In animal models, treatment with the polyclonal or either monoclonal antitoxin provided a statistically significant (p<=0.0001for all three antitoxins) survival benefit compared with no treatment.

nodes.description: Anthrax treatment and postexposure prophylaxis use antibiotics with activity against B. anthracis; ciprofloxacin, doxycycline, levofloxacin, minocycline, penicillin G, and tetracycline are FDA-approved for anthrax PEP, treatment, or both, with broader alternatives in CDC guidance for contraindications, intolerance, limited supply, or engineered resistance.

evidence.reference_title: CDC Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Anthrax, 2023.
evidence.snippet: Ciprofloxacin, doxycycline, levofloxacin, minocycline, penicillin G, and tetracycline are approved by FDA for anthrax PEPAbx, treatment, or both

nodes.description: Ingestion (gastrointestinal) anthrax commonly produces massive ascites, which serves as a further reservoir for lethal factor.

evidence.reference_title: CDC Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Anthrax, 2023.
evidence.snippet: Ascites was observed in 52% of adults with ingestion anthrax

nodes.description: Vegetative bacilli that carry the pXO2 plasmid synthesize the polyglutamate capsule, preventing efficient phagocytosis and enabling extracellular proliferation and bacteremia.

evidence.reference_title: CDC Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Anthrax, 2023.
evidence.snippet: The capsule prevents phagocytosis of the vegetative form of B. anthracis by macrophages, allowing it to evade the immune system.

nodes.description: Inhalational anthrax can progress from nonspecific symptoms to a severe toxemic phase with dyspnea.

evidence.reference_title: Human Anthrax: Update of the Diagnosis and Treatment.
evidence.snippet: The disease progresses to the severe phase which is characterized by high fever, toxemia, dyspnea and cyanosis.

nodes.description: Vesicles at the skin inoculation site are surrounded by edema, and face or neck lesions can have extensive edema.

evidence.reference_title: Human Anthrax: Update of the Diagnosis and Treatment.
evidence.snippet: A lesion begins as a pruritic papule and typically progresses to a ring of vesicles surrounded by erythema and edema within 2-4 days

nodes.description: Protective antigen also delivers edema factor into host cells; edema toxin is one of the two secreted exotoxins responsible for the characteristic symptoms of anthrax, and its activity contributes to the tissue edema of anthrax lesions.

evidence.reference_title: Human Anthrax: Update of the Diagnosis and Treatment.
evidence.snippet: The tripartite toxin comprises protective antigen (PA), lethal factor (LF) and edema factor (EF)

evidence.reference_title: Human Anthrax: Update of the Diagnosis and Treatment.
evidence.snippet: The toxins are secreted the during multiplication of the vegetative B. anthracis and are responsible for the characteristic symptoms of anthrax

nodes.description: Cutaneous anthrax lesions progress from a pruritic papule to vesicles and a black eschar over days.

evidence.reference_title: Human Anthrax: Update of the Diagnosis and Treatment.
evidence.snippet: The formation of the eschar its subsequent resolution can take 2-6 weeks, regardless of treatment

nodes.description: Fever is a nonspecific early manifestation across the portal-of-entry forms.

evidence.reference_title: Human Anthrax: Update of the Diagnosis and Treatment.
evidence.snippet: Following an incubation period of 1-7 days, nonspecific initial symptoms including mild fever, fatigue, malaise, myalgia, nonproductive cough and some chest or abdominal pain are seen

nodes.description: Once protective antigen delivers lethal factor into the cytosol, lethal factor cleaves the N-terminus of MAP kinase kinases (MEK1/2/3), disabling MAPK signaling and suppressing innate and adaptive immune responses.

evidence.reference_title: Dynamic S-acylation controls CMG2 maturation extracellular matrix regulation and anthrax toxin susceptibility in vivo.
evidence.snippet: In the cytosol, LF eventually cleaves the N-terminus of MAP kinase kinases such as MEK1, 2 or 3

evidence.reference_title: CDC Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Anthrax, 2023.
evidence.snippet: The two toxins also facilitate immune system evasion by disrupting various immune cell functions (e.g., cellular signaling and cell migration)

nodes.description: Lethal toxin causes apoptosis of vascular endothelial cells, contributing to hemorrhage and the capillary leak of systemic anthrax.

evidence.reference_title: CDC Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Anthrax, 2023.
evidence.snippet: Lethal toxin causes apoptosis of endothelial cells within the vascular system and is thought to contribute to hemorrhage

nodes.description: Regional and systemic lymphadenopathy occurs across anthrax forms and is associated with early fatal outcomes.

evidence.reference_title: CDC Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Anthrax, 2023.
evidence.snippet: Lymphadenopathy was associated with fatal outcomes within the first 3 days of hospitalization, and abdominal pain was associated with later fatal outcomes

nodes.description: B. anthracis dissemination can produce anthrax meningitis as a complication of any portal-of-entry form.

evidence.reference_title: CDC Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Anthrax, 2023.
evidence.snippet: Anthrax meningitis can complicate any form of anthrax or occur alone.

nodes.description: Inhalational anthrax characteristically produces large pleural effusions rich in anthrax lethal factor.

evidence.reference_title: CDC Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Anthrax, 2023.
evidence.snippet: pleural effusion was most commonly a complication of inhalation anthrax (76%)

nodes.description: Drainage of the large, lethal-factor-rich pleural effusions of inhalational anthrax by thoracentesis or chest-tube placement relieves mechanical lung compression and removes a reservoir of anthrax lethal factor, and is associated with improved survival.

evidence.reference_title: CDC Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Anthrax, 2023.
evidence.snippet: drainage of pleural fluid is believed to improve survival by decreasing mechanical lung compression

evidence.reference_title: Human Anthrax: Update of the Diagnosis and Treatment.
evidence.snippet: this procedure improved outcomes in a series of cases by decreasing the level of lethal factors and mechanical lung compression

nodes.description: Anthrax vaccination is paired with antimicrobial postexposure prophylaxis after exposure of an unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated person so delayed spore germination can be covered after antimicrobial therapy stops.

evidence.reference_title: CDC Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Anthrax, 2023.
evidence.snippet: For unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated persons exposed to B. anthracis, PEP includes both antimicrobial drugs with activity against B. anthracis (PEPAbx) and anthrax vaccine (PEPVx).

nodes.description: Protective antigen binds host anthrax toxin receptors such as ANTXR2/CMG2 and mediates entry of lethal factor and edema factor into toxin-sensitive host cells by endocytic uptake.

evidence.reference_title: Dynamic S-acylation controls CMG2 maturation extracellular matrix regulation and anthrax toxin susceptibility in vivo.
evidence.snippet: CMG2/ANTXR2 functions as a Collagen VI receptor required for extracellular matrix homeostasis and as the primary portal for anthrax toxin entry.

nodes.description: Reaccumulating pleural effusions in inhalational anthrax can cause respiratory failure severe enough to require mechanical ventilation.

evidence.reference_title: Human Anthrax: Update of the Diagnosis and Treatment.
evidence.snippet: In inhalation anthrax, patients may require mechanical ventilation due to respiratory failure caused by reaccumulating pleural effusions.

nodes.description: Each portal-of-entry form can disseminate and progress to anthrax sepsis.

evidence.reference_title: Case report: Cutaneous anthrax diagnosed using mNGS of a formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue sample.
evidence.snippet: The disease has four typical clinical forms, cutaneous, gastrointestinal, inhalation, and injection, all of which may result in sepsis or meningitis

nodes.description: Progressive systemic toxemia culminates in shock, the terminal event across severe anthrax forms.

evidence.reference_title: Human Anthrax: Update of the Diagnosis and Treatment.
evidence.snippet: massive ascites followed by toxemia and shock which results in death

nodes.description: Dormant endospores enter through skin, gut, lung, or injection-site tissue, are engulfed by regional macrophages, and germinate to vegetative bacilli during the first intracellular stage of infection.

evidence.reference_title: Early Bacillus anthracis-macrophage interactions: intracellular survival survival and escape.
evidence.snippet: Anthrax infections are initiated by dormant endospores gaining access to the mammalian host and becoming engulfed by regional macrophages (Mphi).

nodes.description: Toxin-driven immune suppression and continued vegetative growth allow unchecked proliferation and systemic toxemia.

evidence.reference_title: CDC Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Anthrax, 2023.
evidence.snippet: These combined effects allow bacterial proliferation and lead to the high morbidity and mortality associated with anthrax.

nodes.description: Fever, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and diarrhea are early intestinal anthrax symptoms.

evidence.reference_title: Human Anthrax: Update of the Diagnosis and Treatment.
evidence.snippet: The initial symptoms of intestinal anthrax include fever, nausea, vomiting, anorexia and diarrhea.

nodes.description: Newly vegetative bacilli escape from macrophage phagocytic vesicles into the cytoplasm, and that macrophage-release phenotype requires the pXO1 transactivator atxA even when the toxin genes themselves are absent.

evidence.reference_title: Early Bacillus anthracis-macrophage interactions: intracellular survival survival and escape.
evidence.snippet: Genetic analysis from this study indicates that the toxin plasmid pXO1 is required for release from the Mphi, whereas the capsule plasmid pXO2 is not.
